title: Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 2: understanding the self and learning to act
excerpt: An original meaning and detailed contextual explanation of all 72 verses in the Gita’s second chapter.
introHtml:
Krishna rebukes Arjuna’s refusal to fight and teaches that the self is eternal while bodies perish. He then appeals to Arjuna’s duty as a kshatriya and tells him to fight without attachment to gain, loss, victory or defeat. The chapter explains action without desire for its fruits and concludes with the characteristics of a person whose wisdom is steady.

Each Meaning renders the Sanskrit in English. Each Explanation follows the verse’s statements, terms and argument. Named traditional interpretations are distinguished where they differ. [1–3]

verses.meaningHtml: Sanjaya said: To Arjuna, overcome by compassion and distress, his troubled eyes filled with tears, Madhusudana spoke these words.
verses.explanationHtml: Sanjaya describes Arjuna as overcome by compassion, with tear-filled eyes and a sorrowing mind. Krishna, called Madhusudana, then speaks to him. The verse carries the condition described at the end of Chapter 1 into the exchange between Krishna and Arjuna.

verses.meaningHtml: The Blessed Lord said: Arjuna, how has this confusion come upon you at such a crisis? It is unworthy of the noble, leads away from heaven and brings dishonour.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna rebukes Arjuna for falling into this dejection at a critical moment. He calls it unworthy of the noble, an obstacle to heaven and a cause of dishonour. These three descriptions condemn the state in which Arjuna has refused to fight. Krishna’s first response is a challenge to that refusal.

verses.meaningHtml: Do not yield to this unmanliness, Partha; it does not befit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and stand up, scorcher of enemies.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna tells Arjuna not to yield to klaibya, unmanliness or impotence, and says it does not befit him. He commands him to abandon weakness of heart and stand up. The address “scorcher of enemies” recalls Arjuna’s prowess as a warrior while rebuking his present collapse.

verses.meaningHtml: Arjuna said: Madhusudana, how can I fight Bhishma and Drona with arrows in battle? They deserve my reverence, destroyer of enemies.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna asks how he can shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, whom he considers worthy of worship. He addresses Krishna as Madhusudana and destroyer of enemies. The question concerns fighting these two revered men, who stand in the opposing army as his elder and teacher.

verses.meaningHtml: It would be better to live here by begging than to kill these great teachers. If I killed these teachers, even though they seek material gain, the pleasures I enjoyed would be stained with their blood.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that begging would be preferable to killing his revered teachers. Even if they seek worldly gain, he would experience the pleasures obtained by killing them as stained with their blood. He therefore rejects the enjoyment of a kingdom won through their deaths.

verses.meaningHtml: We do not know which is better for us: that we conquer them, or that they conquer us. Those sons of Dhritarashtra stand before us; after killing them, we would not wish to live.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna cannot decide whether victory or defeat would be better. Dhritarashtra’s sons stand before him, and he says that after killing them he would not wish to live. Both possible outcomes of the battle therefore trouble him, leaving him unable to determine what should be done.

verses.meaningHtml: My nature is overpowered by the fault of faintheartedness, and my understanding is confused about dharma. I ask you: tell me decisively what would be truly good. I am your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in you.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that weakness has overwhelmed his nature and that his mind is confused about dharma. He asks Krishna to tell him decisively what is best. By declaring himself Krishna’s disciple and taking refuge in him, Arjuna asks to be taught how to resolve his uncertainty.

verses.meaningHtml: I can see nothing that would remove the sorrow drying up my senses, even if I gained a prosperous, unrivalled kingdom on earth or lordship over the gods.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that neither an unrivalled kingdom on earth nor sovereignty over the gods would remove the grief drying up his senses. The greatest earthly and heavenly rewards are included in his refusal. His distress persists even when he imagines possessing everything that victory might bring.

verses.meaningHtml: Sanjaya said: After speaking in this way to Hrishikesha, Gudakesha, the scorcher of enemies, told Govinda, “I will not fight,” and became silent.
verses.explanationHtml: Sanjaya records Arjuna’s words, “I will not fight,” and the silence that follows. Gudakesha and scorcher of enemies name Arjuna; Hrishikesha and Govinda name Krishna. Having asked for instruction, Arjuna remains seated before Krishna with his refusal stated explicitly.

verses.meaningHtml: To that grieving Arjuna, between the two armies, Hrishikesha spoke as if smiling, descendant of Bharata.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna speaks to the sorrowing Arjuna while they remain between the two armies. The phrase “as if smiling” describes Krishna’s expression as he begins his answer. Sanjaya’s brief narration ends here, and the sustained teaching starts with Krishna’s rebuke in the next verse.

verses.meaningHtml: The Blessed Lord said: You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, yet speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for those whose life has departed nor for those who still live.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that Arjuna grieves for those who should not be grieved for while speaking words that sound wise. He states that the learned grieve neither for the living nor for the dead. The explanation that follows distinguishes the eternal self from the body that undergoes death.

verses.meaningHtml: There was never a time when I did not exist, or you, or these rulers; nor shall any of us cease to exist hereafter.
verses.explanationHtml: The claim of continuity includes Krishna, Arjuna and the rulers on both sides. Their approaching bodily deaths do not, in this teaching, amount to the annihilation of their selves. The plural language has been read differently: Shankara explains it through distinct bodies while affirming the unity of the self; Ramanuja takes the distinction between the Lord and individual selves as real. Both readings preserve the verse’s assertion of enduring existence. [3]

verses.meaningHtml: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it comes to another body. A steady person is not bewildered by that passage.
verses.explanationHtml: The embodied self remains through the body’s childhood, youth and old age, and likewise passes into another body. Krishna places rebirth alongside the changes of bodily condition within one life. The discerning person is not bewildered by these changes because the embodied self continues through them.

verses.meaningHtml: Contacts with objects of sense, son of Kunti, bring cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and are impermanent; endure them, descendant of Bharata.
verses.explanationHtml: Contact between the senses and their objects produces cold and heat, pleasure and pain. Krishna says these experiences come and go and therefore lack permanence. His instruction is to endure them. Their transience is contrasted with the enduring self described in the preceding verses.

verses.meaningHtml: The steady person whom these experiences do not unsettle, who remains even in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality, foremost of men.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna describes the steadfast person who is not disturbed by sensory contacts and remains equal in pleasure and pain. Such a person becomes fit for immortality. Endurance and equanimity are thus connected with liberation, the attainment toward which the teaching about the imperishable self is directed.

verses.meaningHtml: What is unreal has no enduring being; what is real never ceases to be. Those who see the truth have discerned the boundary between them.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna distinguishes sat, what is real or existent, from asat, what is unreal or non-existent. The former does not cease to be, and the latter has no enduring existence. He says that the seers of truth have understood the distinction. The surrounding verses apply it to the imperishable self and perishable bodies.

verses.meaningHtml: Know as indestructible that by which all this is pervaded. No one can bring about the destruction of that imperishable reality.
verses.explanationHtml: What pervades all this is declared indestructible. No one can bring about the destruction of that imperishable reality. The statement continues the distinction of 2.16 and supplies the basis for the contrast between the eternal embodied self and bodies that come to an end in 2.18.

verses.meaningHtml: These bodies of the eternal, indestructible and immeasurable embodied self are said to have an end. Therefore fight, descendant of Bharata.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that bodies perish, while the embodied self is eternal, indestructible and beyond measurement. He then commands Arjuna to fight. The reasoning connects the self’s imperishability directly with the battlefield: the deaths of the bodies before Arjuna do not destroy the self.

verses.meaningHtml: The one who thinks this self kills, and the one who thinks it is killed, both fail to understand. It neither kills nor is killed.
verses.explanationHtml: Both the person who thinks the self kills and the person who thinks it is killed are said not to understand it. Krishna states that the self neither kills nor is killed. Killing and being killed are here denied of the imperishable self, whose distinction from the body was stated in 2.18.

verses.meaningHtml: The self is never born and never dies. Having existed, it does not subsequently cease to exist. Unborn, eternal, enduring and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.
verses.explanationHtml: Several descriptions reinforce one point from different directions. Birth and death belong to a sequence of changes; Krishna describes the self as standing outside that sequence. “Ancient” does not make it an unusually old bodily object: the accompanying “unborn” and “eternal” define the intended sense. The last line returns to the immediate fear raised by the battle, distinguishing the destruction of the body from the destruction of its enduring subject.

verses.meaningHtml: Partha, when someone knows the self as indestructible, eternal, unborn and imperishable, how could that person kill anyone or cause anyone to be killed?
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna asks how someone who knows the self to be imperishable, eternal, unborn and unchanging could kill anyone or cause anyone to be killed. The question follows from the self’s nature described in 2.19–20: it is neither the agent of killing nor the being destroyed when a body dies.

verses.meaningHtml: As a person discards worn-out clothes and puts on other, new ones, so the embodied self discards worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.
verses.explanationHtml: The self’s change of bodies is compared to a person discarding worn clothes and putting on new ones. The wearer continues while the garments change; likewise, the embodied self leaves an old body and takes another. The simile states the continuity of the self through death and rebirth.

verses.meaningHtml: Weapons do not cut this self; fire does not burn it. Water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it.
verses.explanationHtml: Weapons cannot cut the self, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it and wind cannot dry it. Krishna denies that these means of altering or destroying material things can affect the self. The statement specifies the indestructibility asserted in the preceding verses.

verses.meaningHtml: The self cannot be cut, burned, wetted or dried. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable and everlasting.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna repeats the self’s immunity to cutting, burning, wetting and drying, then calls it eternal, all-pervading, stable, unmoving and everlasting. These descriptions distinguish the self from bodies that change and perish. Its permanence is the basis of his instruction that Arjuna should not grieve for it.

verses.meaningHtml: The self is said to be unmanifest, beyond ordinary thought and unchanging. Knowing it in this way, you should not grieve.
verses.explanationHtml: The self is described as unmanifest, inconceivable and unchanging. It cannot be grasped as a visible, changing object. Krishna says that knowing the self in this way removes the reason to grieve for it. The conclusion continues the argument that bodily death leaves the self undestroyed.

verses.meaningHtml: Even if you think the self is continually born and continually dies, mighty-armed one, you still should not grieve in this way.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna considers the alternative supposition that the self is continually born and continually dies. Even on that assumption, he tells Arjuna that he should not grieve. The following verses give the reason: birth and death would still be unavoidable consequences of one another.

verses.meaningHtml: For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain. Therefore you should not grieve over what cannot be avoided.
verses.explanationHtml: For one who has been born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain. Krishna uses this inevitability as the reason Arjuna should not grieve. The verse continues the preceding argument about recurring birth and death and what cannot be prevented within that cycle.

verses.meaningHtml: Beings are unmanifest at their beginning, manifest in their middle, and unmanifest again at their end, descendant of Bharata. What occasion for lamentation is there in this?
verses.explanationHtml: Beings are unmanifest before their appearance, manifest during the intervening span, and unmanifest again when that span ends. Krishna asks what cause for lamentation there is in this sequence. Visible bodily existence is presented as the middle stage between two unmanifest conditions.

verses.meaningHtml: One person sees the self as a wonder; another speaks of it as a wonder; another hears of it as a wonder. Someone may hear of it and still not truly know it.
verses.explanationHtml: The self is seen, described and heard of as a wonder. Yet hearing about it does not necessarily bring understanding. Krishna distinguishes the extraordinary character of the self from the different ways people encounter its teaching. The following verse concludes the argument by again declaring the embodied self indestructible.

verses.meaningHtml: The embodied self in everyone’s body is always beyond being killed, descendant of Bharata. Therefore you should not grieve for any being.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that the embodied self in every body can never be killed. The statement includes the selves of all the warriors before Arjuna. He therefore tells Arjuna not to grieve for any being. This concludes the account of the self before the discussion turns to his duty as a kshatriya.

verses.meaningHtml: Considering your own dharma as well, you should not waver. For a kshatriya, there is nothing higher than a righteous battle.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna now appeals to Arjuna’s svadharma, his own duty as a kshatriya. He says that nothing is higher for a kshatriya than a righteous battle and tells him not to waver. The argument adds warrior duty to the preceding teaching that bodily death does not destroy the self.

verses.meaningHtml: Happy are the kshatriyas who encounter a battle of this kind that comes to them unsought, Partha: an open doorway to heaven.
verses.explanationHtml: The righteous battle is compared to an open gate of heaven. Krishna calls those kshatriyas fortunate who encounter such a battle without seeking it. Heaven is named directly as the reward associated with this opportunity to fulfil the warrior’s duty described in 2.31.

verses.meaningHtml: But if you do not undertake this righteous battle, you will abandon your own dharma and honour, and incur wrongdoing.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that refusing this righteous battle would mean abandoning Arjuna’s own duty and honour and would bring sin upon him. Arjuna had argued that fighting his relatives would be sinful. Krishna now states the opposing conclusion: in these circumstances, failure to fight would itself incur sin.

verses.meaningHtml: People will speak of your lasting dishonour. For someone who has been held in esteem, dishonour is worse than death.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna warns that people will speak of Arjuna’s dishonour for a long time. For a man who has been honoured, he says, disgrace is worse than death. The argument presses the consequences of abandoning battle through the loss of Arjuna’s reputation.

verses.meaningHtml: The great chariot-warriors will think you withdrew from battle through fear. Those who once held you in high regard will come to regard you lightly.
verses.explanationHtml: The great chariot-warriors will interpret Arjuna’s withdrawal as fear. Those who once esteemed him will cease to do so. Krishna contrasts Arjuna’s reasons for refusing battle with the judgement the other warriors will make of that refusal.

verses.meaningHtml: Your enemies will speak many words that should not be spoken, belittling your ability. What could be more painful than that?
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that Arjuna’s enemies will insult him and belittle his fighting ability. He asks what could cause greater pain than hearing those words. This continues the appeal to honour and disgrace begun in 2.33–35.

verses.meaningHtml: If killed, you will attain heaven; if victorious, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore stand up, son of Kunti, determined to fight.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna gives the two possible outcomes of fighting: if Arjuna is killed, he will attain heaven; if he wins, he will enjoy earthly kingship. He then tells him to stand up, resolved to fight. Both outcomes are presented as reasons to undertake the battle.

verses.meaningHtml: Hold pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike; then commit yourself to the battle. Acting in this way, you will not incur wrongdoing.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna tells Arjuna to treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and victory and defeat alike, and then engage in battle. He says that fighting with this evenness will not bring sin upon him. Equanimity in action becomes the connection between the preceding command to fight and the account of yoga that follows.

verses.meaningHtml: This understanding has been explained to you in relation to Sankhya. Now hear it in relation to yoga: joined to this understanding, Partha, you will cast off the bondage of action.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna distinguishes the understanding of the self already explained as Sankhya from the discipline of yoga he will now teach. Joined to this understanding, Arjuna will cast off the bondage of action. The next section explains action performed with steady understanding and without attachment to its fruits.

verses.meaningHtml: In this discipline, no beginning is lost and no contrary setback arises. Even a little of this dharma protects one from great fear.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that a beginning made in this discipline is not lost and does not produce a contrary result. Even a small measure of it protects against great fear. The assurance introduces buddhi-yoga, whose practice and freedom from the bondage of action are described in the following verses.

verses.meaningHtml: Here, descendant of Kuru, resolute understanding is single in its direction. The thoughts of the irresolute are many-branched and without end.
verses.explanationHtml: Resolute understanding has one settled aim, while the thoughts of the irresolute branch endlessly. Krishna contrasts steadiness in the discipline he is teaching with the many pursuits generated by changing desires. The following verses identify promises of ritual reward as a cause of such divided attention.

verses.meaningHtml: Those without discernment, Partha, speak flowery words. They delight in Vedic pronouncements and insist that there is nothing beyond them.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna criticises those who delight in Vedic pronouncements, speak flowery words and insist that there is nothing beyond them. Their words are attractive to those seeking rewards. The sentence continues through 2.43–44, identifying their desires, promised results and the obstruction they cause to resolute understanding.

verses.meaningHtml: Filled with desire and intent on heaven, they speak of many special rites that yield rebirth as the fruit of action and lead toward enjoyment and power.
verses.explanationHtml: The speakers described in 2.42 are filled with desire and regard heaven as their goal. They prescribe many special rites for enjoyment and power, but the fruits of those actions lead to further birth. Krishna connects their ritual promises with desire, action and renewed embodiment.

verses.meaningHtml: For those attached to enjoyment and power, whose minds are carried away by such speech, resolute understanding does not become established in concentration.
verses.explanationHtml: Attachment to enjoyment and power prevents resolute understanding from becoming established in concentration. The minds of these people have been carried away by the flowery promises just described. The verse completes the sentence of 2.42–44 by stating how desire for ritual rewards obstructs the discipline Krishna is teaching.

verses.meaningHtml: The Vedas concern the three gunas; rise beyond the three gunas, Arjuna. Be free from the pairs of opposites, steadfast in clarity, without anxiety over acquisition and preservation, and established in the self.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that the Vedas concern the three gunas and tells Arjuna to go beyond them. He adds the commands to be free from the pairs of opposites, remain steadfast in clarity, abandon concern for acquiring and preserving possessions, and be established in the self. These instructions turn from the pursuit of rewards to freedom from attachment.

verses.meaningHtml: For the brahmin who understands, all the Vedas have the usefulness of a well when water is available on every side.
verses.explanationHtml: A well supplies particular needs, but when water is abundant on every side its use is fulfilled within that abundance. Krishna compares this with the usefulness of all the Vedas for the brahmin who has understanding. The comparison places comprehensive knowledge above dependence on the separate benefits described in the preceding ritual promises.

verses.meaningHtml: Your sphere is action alone, never its fruits. Do not make the fruit of action your motive, and do not become attached to inaction.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna assigns Arjuna action as his sphere, while denying him a claim to its fruits. The result is not to be his motive, and he is also forbidden attachment to inaction. All four instructions belong together: perform the action, relinquish the fruit, and do not make relinquishment a reason to stop acting.

verses.meaningHtml: Established in yoga, perform your actions while relinquishing attachment, Dhananjaya. Remain even in success and failure: this evenness is called yoga.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna is told to act while established in yoga and to relinquish attachment. The same evenness is to be maintained whether the action succeeds or fails. Krishna explicitly calls this equality yoga. It continues the instruction of 2.47 by identifying the disposition in which action is to be performed.

verses.meaningHtml: Action pursued for its fruits is far lower than the yoga of understanding, Dhananjaya. Seek refuge in understanding; those who make results their motive are pitiable.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna calls action pursued for its fruits inferior to buddhi-yoga and tells Arjuna to seek refuge in understanding. Those who make results their motive are described as pitiable. The comparison continues the contrast between fruit-seeking action and the even understanding defined in 2.48.

verses.meaningHtml: One joined to understanding leaves behind both good and bad karmic results here. Therefore devote yourself to yoga: yoga is skill in actions.
verses.explanationHtml: “Skill” is defined by the preceding account of understanding, attachment and freedom from bondage. It is the capacity to engage in action without becoming bound through the appropriation of its results. The reference to good and bad results includes merit as well as wrongdoing, because even desirable karmic rewards can continue the cycle of birth. The verse gives action a place within liberation by explaining how its relation to the agent can be transformed.

verses.meaningHtml: The wise who are joined to understanding relinquish the fruit born of action. Freed from the bondage of birth, they reach the condition beyond affliction.
verses.explanationHtml: The wise relinquish the fruits born of action and are released from the bondage of birth. They attain the state beyond affliction. Krishna therefore gives liberation from repeated embodiment as the outcome of the discipline, continuing the claim in 2.50 that understanding frees one from both good and bad karmic consequences.

verses.meaningHtml: When your understanding has crossed the tangled thicket of delusion, you will become dispassionate toward what has been heard and what remains to be heard.
verses.explanationHtml: The thicket image conveys entanglement: directions multiply until the person cannot see a way through. Crossing it changes the force of competing promises and prescriptions. In the context of 2.42–46, what has been heard includes teachings approached as a means of acquiring desired results. Dispassion develops when a clearer understanding of the aim has emerged. The verse prepares the distinction between being pulled about by reports and becoming steadily established in insight.

verses.meaningHtml: When your understanding, bewildered by what it has heard, stands unmoving and steady in concentration, then you will attain yoga.
verses.explanationHtml: The movement from scattered hearing to stable understanding is completed here. Different formulations and promised outcomes have been pulling attention in different directions. Yoga is attained when that agitation gives way to a settled orientation. Arjuna responds by asking what such a person is like in ordinary conduct. The dialogue thus moves from the description of an inward discipline to the question of how its maturity appears in speaking, sitting and moving.

verses.meaningHtml: Arjuna said: Keshava, how is someone of settled wisdom, established in concentration, described? How does such a steady-minded person speak, sit and move?
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna asks for recognisable characteristics, bringing the account of understanding into the world of conduct. His questions combine the description of a person with the activities through which a life is ordinarily observed. The answer will range beyond outward postures to desire, emotional steadiness, sense-restraint and the relation to possessions. This makes the remainder of the chapter a portrait of disciplined understanding expressed in living.

verses.meaningHtml: The Blessed Lord said: When a person gives up all desires that arise in the mind, Partha, and is content in the self through the self, that person is called one of settled wisdom.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna begins his description of steady wisdom with the abandonment of all desires arising in the mind. Such a person is satisfied in the self through the self. Contentment is thus located in the self itself, and this freedom from desire supplies the first answer to Arjuna’s question in 2.54.

verses.meaningHtml: One whose mind is not shaken by suffering, who does not crave pleasure, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger is called a sage of steady understanding.
verses.explanationHtml: A sage of steady wisdom is not disturbed by suffering and does not crave pleasures. Attachment, fear and anger have departed. Krishna describes steadiness through the absence of these responses, extending the abandonment of desire stated in 2.55 to painful and pleasurable experiences alike.

verses.meaningHtml: One who clings nowhere, and who neither exults nor hates on meeting favourable and unfavourable conditions, has firmly established wisdom.
verses.explanationHtml: The person of established wisdom is attached to nothing and neither welcomes what is favourable nor hates what is unfavourable. Encounters with good and bad fortune continue, but they no longer produce rejoicing and aversion. This applies the evenness of 2.56 to what a person meets.

verses.meaningHtml: When a person withdraws the senses from their objects on every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, that person’s wisdom is firmly established.
verses.explanationHtml: The tortoise supplies an image of the capacity to withdraw. The senses need not always be carried outward by whatever appears before them. This capacity supports the steadiness of understanding by giving attention a degree of independence from immediate stimulation. The simile describes an available movement of restraint. Later verses also describe moving among sense objects with disciplined senses, so the chapter’s portrait includes both withdrawal and well-governed engagement.

verses.meaningHtml: Objects of sense recede from an embodied person who abstains, although the taste for them remains. Even that taste ceases when the higher reality is seen.
verses.explanationHtml: The verse distinguishes a change in outward contact from a change in attraction. Abstinence can remove an object from immediate experience while leaving an inward relish for it intact. The word rasa, taste, makes that remaining pull vivid. In the teaching, a deeper apprehension of the higher reality changes what the object promises to provide. This explains why restraint and knowledge work together in the preceding account of steady understanding.

verses.meaningHtml: Even for a discerning person who strives, son of Kunti, the turbulent senses can forcibly carry the mind away.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna warns that the turbulent senses can forcibly carry away even the mind of a discerning person who is making an effort. Understanding and effort do not by themselves place the senses under control. The warning leads directly to the command to restrain them and remain devoted to Krishna in 2.61.

verses.meaningHtml: Having restrained them all, a person should remain collected, with me as the highest aim. Wisdom is firmly established in the one whose senses are under control.
verses.explanationHtml: The verse gives restraint a positive orientation: Krishna himself is to be held as the highest aim. Devotion is therefore already present within this early account of disciplined understanding. The senses are gathered around a direction that gives their restraint purpose. In the dialogue, this helps connect knowledge of the self, control of attention and the relation between Arjuna and his teacher. These themes will become increasingly explicit in later chapters.

verses.meaningHtml: When a person dwells on sense objects, attachment to them arises. From attachment comes desire, and from desire comes anger.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna traces a sequence beginning with repeated attention. Dwelling on an object makes it increasingly important to one’s imagined fulfilment; attachment then becomes a demand to obtain or retain it. Anger arises within that movement when the demand meets an obstacle. The verse describes a pattern through which attention can become bondage. It also shows why earlier verses gave sense-restraint and understanding a place before the moment of overt action.

verses.meaningHtml: From anger comes bewilderment; from bewilderment, the confusion of memory; from confused memory, the ruin of understanding. With understanding ruined, the person is lost.
verses.explanationHtml: Anger produces delusion; delusion disrupts memory; the loss of memory destroys understanding; and when understanding is destroyed, the person perishes. This completes the sequence begun in 2.62 with dwelling on sense objects. Krishna traces how attachment and desire lead, through anger, to the destruction of the faculty that guides conduct.

verses.meaningHtml: But a disciplined person moving among sense objects, with senses governed by the self and free from attraction and aversion, attains tranquillity.
verses.explanationHtml: The portrait now includes movement among objects rather than withdrawal alone. The decisive change is that attraction and aversion no longer govern the encounter. The senses operate within a disciplined orientation, allowing a condition of prasāda: clarity, calm or serenity. This complements the tortoise image in 2.58. The chapter describes capacities needed for a life that must sometimes withdraw attention and sometimes engage with what the world presents.

verses.meaningHtml: In that tranquillity, the ending of all this person’s suffering comes about, for the understanding of one whose mind is clear soon becomes firmly established.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that serenity brings the destruction of all suffering. In a serene mind, understanding soon becomes firmly established. The verse states the result of the disciplined movement among sense objects described in 2.64: freedom from attraction and aversion leads to serenity and steadiness of understanding.

verses.meaningHtml: For one who is uncollected there is no settled understanding, and no sustained contemplation. Without contemplation there is no peace; without peace, where can happiness be?
verses.explanationHtml: Without collectedness there is neither understanding nor sustained contemplation; without contemplation there is no peace. Krishna then asks how there could be happiness for someone without peace. The verse gives a sequence of dependence linking disciplined concentration, understanding, contemplation, peace and happiness.

verses.meaningHtml: When the mind follows the wandering senses, it carries away a person’s wisdom as a wind carries a boat away on the water.
verses.explanationHtml: The boat image makes the loss of direction concrete. The senses can encounter many objects, but a mind that simply follows their movement loses the ability to steer. The danger is therefore described through the relation between movement and guidance. This gives another explanation of the sequence in 2.62–63. The point of restraint is to preserve the governing place of understanding while the person continues to meet a changing world.

verses.meaningHtml: Therefore, mighty-armed one, the person whose senses are restrained on every side from their objects has firmly established wisdom.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna draws together the examples of turbulence, withdrawal and steering. “On every side” answers the many directions in which attention can be captured. The repeated phrase about established wisdom returns to Arjuna’s question in 2.54, giving sense-restraint a clear place within the answer. The title “mighty-armed” also recalls Arjuna’s familiar strength, while the discipline now being discussed requires a corresponding steadiness in the governance of attention.

verses.meaningHtml: What is night for all beings is a time of wakefulness for the self-restrained person. What is wakefulness for beings is night for the sage who sees.
verses.explanationHtml: What is night for all beings is the time of wakefulness for the self-controlled sage. What occupies the wakefulness of other beings is night for the sage who sees. The reversed images distinguish the sage’s knowledge of the self from ordinary preoccupation with sense objects.

verses.meaningHtml: As waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains firmly established, so all desires enter such a person. That person attains peace; the one who longs for desires does not.
verses.explanationHtml: The ocean remains full and unmoved while rivers enter it. Krishna compares it to the person into whom desires enter without disturbing peace. The person who desires their fulfilment does not attain that peace. The contrast continues the portrait of one whose wisdom remains steady amid the presence of sense objects.

verses.meaningHtml: The person who gives up all desires, moves without craving, and is free from possessiveness and ego-centred claiming attains peace.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna describes one who abandons all desires and moves without longing, possessiveness or egoism. “Without mine” denies the claim of ownership; “without I” denies egoistic self-identification. Such a person attains peace. These traits complete the portrait that began in 2.55 with satisfaction in the self.

verses.meaningHtml: This is the state grounded in Brahman, Partha. On attaining it, one is no longer deluded. Remaining in it even at the time of death, one reaches liberation in Brahman.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna calls this the state grounded in Brahman. Having attained it, a person is no longer deluded; remaining established in it even at death, one reaches liberation in Brahman. The chapter closes by identifying the final attainment of the steady understanding and desirelessness described in the preceding verses.
